request.job_description: We are hiring an Applied AI Engineer to build and ship LLM-powered features in our product. You will design retrieval-augmented generation pipelines, build evaluation harnesses to measure quality and regressions, and write production Python services. You will work with product and design to turn ambiguous user needs into reliable features, and own quality, latency and cost in production.

transcript.question: Walk me through a RAG system you built end to end. What were the key design decisions?
transcript.answer: I built a support-answering assistant over about 40,000 help-center and internal docs. I started with fixed 1,000-token chunks and plain dense retrieval, and recall was poor on queries with product names and error codes. I moved to heading-aware chunks of roughly 300 to 500 tokens with overlap, added BM25 alongside embeddings with reciprocal rank fusion, and put a cross-encoder reranker on the top 30. Recall@10 on our labelled set went from 0.64 to 0.87. The reranker added about 120 ms, which we accepted after checking p95 latency stayed under our 2.5 second budget. I also added metadata filters by product version because stale docs were causing wrong answers.

transcript.question: How did you evaluate whether the assistant was actually good, and how did you catch regressions?
transcript.answer: We had a golden set of around 300 questions that support agents helped label. I tracked retrieval recall and also an answer-quality score. For answer quality we ran an LLM judge, and I would say it generally worked well. We ran it before releases. I think we looked at the scores and if they looked okay we shipped. I didn't really calibrate the judge against humans, though that would be a good thing to do.

transcript.question: Tell me about how you structure Python code for an LLM service going to production.
transcript.answer: I usually use FastAPI and keep things in modules, with the retrieval part and the generation part separate. I use async for the model calls. I write some tests, mostly for the parsing functions. For deployment, it was handled by another team, so I'm not very familiar with the details.

transcript.question: Describe a time you had to work with a product manager or non-technical stakeholder who had unrealistic expectations of the LLM feature.
transcript.answer: The PM wanted the assistant to never be wrong and wanted to launch to all customers at once. I explained that hallucinations can't be eliminated entirely and showed them the 15 failure cases from our golden set, grouped by cause. We agreed on a staged rollout: internal agents first, then 10 percent of customers, with a thumbs-down button and an 'I'm not sure, here are the sources' fallback when the reranker score was below a threshold. Escalation to humans dropped by roughly a quarter in the pilot, and the PM later used the failure categories to prioritize doc fixes with the content team.

transcript.question: If your retrieval quality suddenly dropped in production, how would you debug it?
transcript.answer: I would check whether the documents or embeddings changed, like a re-index or a new embedding model version. Then I'd look at logged queries to see if the query distribution shifted, and compare retrieval results on the golden set against last week's. I'd also check the metadata filters since version filters broke us once. Honestly I haven't set up automated monitoring for this, so I'd be doing it by hand.
